title: Styles of turban
hookLine: many styles, from the everyday pagg to the tall dumalla

cards: Stand at the door of a big gurdwara on a festival morning and watch the heads come in. A neat, pointed turban in deep navy. A rounded one in bright saffron.
A small cloth knotted on a boy's head. A tall, wound turban in dark blue, with a steel emblem fixed at the front. Pink at a wedding.
White on an older man. Patterned cloth on a young woman. Same faith, same hall, same Guru at the front.
Yesterday ended with the covering; today, the covering itself.

teach.b: Begin with the everyday one. In Punjabi it's often just called the pagg, and its formal name is dastar: a long strip of cloth, folded and wound around the head in layers, finished neatly.
Families and regions tie it differently, one to a sharp peak at the front, another rounder and softer, and people often learn the style of a father, an uncle or a friend. Next, the smaller coverings.
A patka is a square of cloth tied over the hair knot, often worn by children before they learn the full turban, and by some for sport.
A keski is a shorter turban, worn by some under a larger one, and by some, including some Sikh women who wear a turban, on its own.
Then the tall one. The dumalla is wound high and full, sometimes with a steel emblem or small weapons tucked into it.
It's closely tied to the Nihangs, the Sikh order known for keeping the old martial dress, and others wear it too.
Color is mostly choice: some match a shirt, some wear saffron or blue on festival days, some wear one color for years. Here's what joins them.
Earlier on this path, the code asked the turban of Sikh men and left it open to women, and your line was crowned.

teach.h: TALL OR NEAT, STILL A CROWN.
teach.b: A crown can be tall or neat, bright or plain, and still be a crown.
So the week closes: Patna and Hazur Sahib, the Sarbat Khalsa, the old rehatnamas, why a written code, caring for kesh, and now the turban itself.

how: Sikhs tie turbans in many styles, from the everyday pagg to the tall dumalla, often learning a style from family, and children often begin with a patka.

games.q: a boy at the gurdwara is too young to tie a full turban yet. what does he often wear?
o: a patka tied over the hair knot.
games.why: a patka is often worn by children before they learn the full turban, and by some people for sport.

practice: Bring to mind the turbans you've seen, on a street, on a screen, at a gurdwara, or look at a few pictures if you can. Notice each one without judging: the shape, the color, the care in the folds.
Then notice the person under it, who wound that cloth this morning, layer by layer, with their own hands.

wordCard.voice: Styles of turban. Many ways to tie it, from the everyday pagg to the tall dumalla, each one the same crown. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: the tall, full wound turban.

carryVoice: Your line: many styles, one crown. Tall or neat, bright or plain, the meaning holds. That's the week.
